question: Does the federal Pay Equity Act set up a proactive process for every employer in Canada?
generated_answer:
No, the federal Pay Equity Act does not set up a proactive process for every employer in Canada. It applies specifically to federally regulated employers, which include certain industries such as banking, telecommunications, and transportation, as well as federal public service employees. These employers are required to implement pay equity plans to identify and address gender-based pay disparities. However, the Act does not apply to private sector employers outside of these federally regulated industries, nor does it require all employers to proactively implement pay equity plans. Instead, it sets out a framework for federally regulated employers to follow in order to achieve pay equity. For other employers, pay equity is often addressed through provincial or territorial legislation, collective agreements, or voluntary employer initiatives. 

In 2021, the federal government introduced the Pay Equity Act, which requires federally regulated employers with 10 or more employees to implement pay equity plans. The Act aims to address gender-based pay disparities by requiring employers to:

1. Identify job classes in their workplace.
2. Determine the value of work in those job classes, taking into account factors such as skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions.
3. Compare the compensation of predominantly female job classes with predominantly male job classes of similar value.
4. Identify and address any pay disparities that are found to be gender-based.

The Act also establishes a Pay Equity Commissioner, who is responsible for enforcing the Act and providing guidance to employers. Employers are required to post their pay equity plans and progress reports on a public registry, which helps to increase transparency and accountability.

While the federal Pay Equity Act does not apply to all employers in Canada, it sets an important precedent and can influence pay equity practices in other sectors. Some provinces and territories have their own pay equity legislation, which may apply to a broader range of employers. For example, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia have pay equity laws that apply to most employers in those provinces, including private sector employers.

In summary, the federal Pay Equity Act sets up a proactive process for federally regulated employers to address gender-based pay disparities, but it does not apply universally to all employers in Canada. Other employers may be subject to pay equity requirements under provincial or territorial legislation, collective agreements, or voluntary employer initiatives. 

If you are an employer or employee in a non-federally regulated industry, you should check with your provincial or territorial government to determine if there are specific pay equity requirements that apply to your workplace. Additionally, many employers choose to implement pay equity practices voluntarily, even if they are not required to do so by law, as part of their commitment to fairness, diversity, and inclusion. 

For more information on pay equity in your specific province or territory, you can visit the website of your provincial or territorial human rights commission or labour ministry.

- Pay Equity Commissioner: [https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/equality/pay-equity.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/equality/pay-equity.html)
- Provincial and territorial pay equity resources:
  - Ontario: [https://www.ontario.ca/page/pay-equity](https://www.ontario.ca/page/pay-equity)
  - Quebec: [https://www.cdpdj.qc.ca/en/rights/equality/pay-equity](https://www.cdpdj.qc.ca/en/rights/equality/pay-equity)
  - British Columbia: [https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/employment-business/employment-standards-advice/employment-standards/equal-pay](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/employment-business/employment-standards-advice/employment-standards/equal-pay) 

Please note that the availability and content of these resources may change over time, so it's always a good idea to check the most up-to-date information from the relevant government websites.
